narrative:
The model predicted a 62.6% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability exceeded the school's acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.40 was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. Although this GPA is higher than the average of accepted students (3.23), the model determined that it still signaled a higher risk of struggling with the bar exam. 

Next, your strong performance in your third year of law school worked in your favor. Placing in the 9th decile far exceeded the average of about 5.8 among accepted students, and this achievement pulled the prediction toward passing. However, it was not enough to overcome the other factors.

Finally, your upper-middle family income also contributed toward predicting failure. While this background is common among accepted students (45% of them come from the same bracket), the model associated it with a slightly elevated risk in this specific combination of traits.

Taken together, these elements led the system to conclude you were more likely than not to fail the bar exam. To improve your chances in future applications, consider strengthening areas the model views as risk factors, such as through additional bar-prep coursework or targeted practice that demonstrates your ability to convert solid grades into exam success. Reapply once you have new evidence of first-time bar passage readiness. (248 words)
